cases.subject: History
cases.wording:
Today, every child in Britain has to be at school, and nobody pays you to come.

Queen Victoria was on the throne from 1837 to 1901. For most of that time, no law said a child had to be in school. Poor families needed every penny, and a child's wage was part of it.

Look at their boots and their clothes. Nobody here is on the way to school.

cases.subject: History
cases.wording:
We know Victorian children went out to work because their families needed the money. Thousands of them went underground, into the coal mines.

A hurrier pushed and pulled wagons full of coal, called corves, along the tunnels. Patience Kershaw pushed hers with her head, over and over, until the hair wore away.

Patience was seventeen when she spoke to the inspectors in 1842. Children as young as eight were hurrying coal in the same pits.

cases.subject: History
cases.wording: She went down at five in the morning and came out at five at night. What was left of her day?

cases.subject: History
cases.wording: Every part has her own words attached to it.

cases.subject: History
cases.wording:
How long she worked: five o'clock in the morning until five in the evening. "I go at five o'clock in the morning and come out at five in the evening."

How hard or dangerous it was: she pushed heavy coal wagons a mile and more, with her head. "I hurry the corves a mile and more under ground and back." "The bald place upon my head is made by thrusting the corves."

How she was treated: she was beaten when she was too slow. "Sometimes they beat me, if I am not quick enough."
